subject: unilateral-mistake
note:
READ THE `searches` ARRAY BEFORE THE `entries` ARRAY. This sweep is NARROW and its narrowness is the most important thing about it. ONE full-text query was run against ONE corpus of SINGAPORE judgments. There was NO sweep of English, Australian or American materials at all -- not of later authority, not of academic criticism, not of anything -- so the three comparator modules rest on a 2005 Singapore judgment's account of them with nothing checking whether those accounts are still good. An entry absent from this register is not an entry that does not exist.

Five later Singapore decisions citing the doctrine were FOUND and are recorded. One (Quoine) was read in full and is encoded. FOUR WERE NOT READ, and are dispositioned `deferred` rather than `no-effect`, because 'I did not open it' and 'it does not affect the encoding' are different statements and only one of them is true here.

A judgment carries no amendment or commencement markers, so the source bundle declares no `annotations` and `dispositions` below is empty. That is a structural fact about judge-made law, not an omission: there is no marker inventory for this stage to dispose of.

A VOCABULARY MISMATCH, RECORDED RATHER THAN FUDGED. This register's `class` and `binding_effect` fields were designed for a STATUTE being amended: the binding effects it admits are struck, stayed, read-down, restricted, added and substituted. None of them describes what a later court does to a judge-made doctrine when it restates it unchanged, which is what Quoine (2020) did and what makes it worth recording at all. Both Quoine and Donovan are therefore classed `interpretive` -- they tell you how to read the doctrine without modifying any text -- and each is routed to the fork it opens. That is the honest fit, not a workaround: neither decision modified the source this corpus encodes. A `class` value for later authority that confirms, and a `binding_effect` of `affirmed`, would let this be said directly, and are a candidate upstream issue against the schema.

searches.question: What later Singapore authority has applied, restated, doubted or distinguished the unilateral-mistake doctrine in Chwee Kin Keong?
searches.scope: One full-text query -- 'Chwee Kin Keong Digilandmall unilateral mistake equity' -- against the lawplain Singapore judgments corpus, limit 10, ranked by relevance.
searches.coverage_note: COVERS: Singapore judgments indexed by that corpus, matching that one query, within the top ten results. DOES NOT COVER: any judgment the query missed or that ranked eleventh or lower; any Singapore decision not in that corpus; ANY English, Australian or United States authority whatsoever; academic commentary; and any legislative change. No second query was run and no citator was consulted, so a case that doubts the doctrine without using these words would not appear.

searches.question: What is the text of Restatement (Second) of Contracts ss 153 and 154, and which American decision adopted it?
searches.scope: One web search for the Restatement text together with Donovan v RRL Corp, followed by retrieval of the Donovan opinion.
searches.coverage_note: COVERS: the text of ss 153 and 154 and one Californian decision adopting s 153(a). DOES NOT COVER: which other States have adopted either section, on what terms, or whether any has since departed from it; later American authority of any kind; and the American Law Institute's own current text, which was not consulted. The American column of the comparison is the Restatement rule and not the law of the United States -- see fork F-US1.

entries.summary: Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd [2020] SGCA(I) 02 -- a five-judge Court of Appeal, fifteen years later, restating the Chwee Kin Keong test and applying it where both parties contracted through algorithms.

provenance.source: lawplain Singapore judgments corpus, then the eLitigation page in full
provenance.citation: Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd [2020] SGCA(I) 02 at [13] and [16]
provenance.quote: The type of knowledge required on the part of the non-mistaken party of the mistaken party's mistake differed depending on whether a party was seeking to invoke the doctrine of unilateral mistake at common law or in equity. The former required proof that the non-mistaken party had actual knowledge of the mistake at the time of the contract, while the latter required constructive knowledge (coupled with an element of unconscionability)

entries.disposition_note: READ IN FULL AND ENCODED. It confirms rather than changes the doctrine, which is itself the finding worth having: the 2005 test is still the test. It is cited in sg-unilateral-mistake.l4 for the term requirement and the knowledge split, and supplies fixture 8. It also OPENS fork F-SG1 by reserving whether equity might reach beyond a mistake as to a term. Only [13] and [16] were read; the judgment is 203,459 characters and the rest of it is not encoded.

entries.summary: Axis Megalink Sdn Bhd v Far East Mining Pte Ltd [2024] SGHC(A) 15 -- the most recent decision found citing the doctrine, on commercial certainty where unilateral mistake is raised.

provenance.source: lawplain Singapore judgments corpus, search result snippet only
provenance.citation: Axis Megalink Sdn Bhd v Far East Mining Pte Ltd [2024] SGHC(A) 15 at [77]
provenance.quote: The reference in the passage just quoted to “commercial certainty” nods to the point that, where unilateral mistake

routing.effective_from_absent_reason: A judgment states the law as from the date it is given; there is no separate effective date, and the currency risk is that this one was not read rather than that its date is unknown.

entries.disposition_note: NOT READ. The snippet shows it engaging with the doctrine's rationale, and it is the newest authority this sweep found -- which makes it the single most likely place for a change the encoding has missed. `deferred` and not `no-effect`: nothing here supports a claim that it leaves the encoding untouched. A reviewer should open this one first.

entries.summary: Wong Chong Hui v Lim Siong Hoe Lawrence [2019] SGHC 85 -- sets out the Digilandmall elements as a numbered list.

provenance.source: lawplain Singapore judgments corpus, search result snippet only
provenance.citation: Wong Chong Hui and another v Lim Siong Hoe Lawrence [2019] SGHC 85
provenance.quote: (a) The respondent must have made a mistake

entries.disposition_note: NOT READ. A High Court decision cannot change what the Court of Appeal held, so it carries little currency risk -- but its enumeration of the elements would be a useful independent check on whether this encoding has the element list right, and that check was not performed.

entries.summary: Broadley Construction Pte Ltd v Alacran Design Pte Ltd [2018] SGCA 25 -- Court of Appeal, considering whether the Chwee Kin Keong requirements were satisfied on the facts.

provenance.source: lawplain Singapore judgments corpus, search result snippet only
provenance.citation: Broadley Construction Pte Ltd v Alacran Design Pte Ltd [2018] SGCA 25
provenance.quote: were satisfied, namely that for a unilateral mistake

routing.effective_from_absent_reason: As for EM-axis: a judgment has no separate effective date, and the risk is that it was not read.

entries.disposition_note: NOT READ, and it is a COURT OF APPEAL decision, which is the level that could refine the test. Second priority for a reviewer after EM-axis.

entries.summary: Olivine Capital Pte Ltd v Chia Chin Yan [2014] SGCA 19 -- treats Chwee Kin Keong as the leading decision, but on COMMON mistake in equity.

provenance.source: lawplain Singapore judgments corpus, search result snippet only
provenance.citation: Olivine Capital Pte Ltd and another v Chia Chin Yan and another matter [2014] SGCA 19
provenance.quote: of common mistake in equity, the leading decision being that of this court in Chwee Kin Keong

entries.disposition_note: NOT READ, and scoped out rather than deferred because the snippet places it on COMMON mistake, which this corpus does not encode. The scope-out rests on the snippet alone; if that characterisation is wrong the case moves to `deferred`.

entries.summary: Donovan v RRL Corp (2001) 26 Cal 4th 261 adopted Restatement s 153(a) as California law and supplies the verbatim text of ss 153 and 154.

provenance.quote: Because the rule in section 153, subdivision (a), of the Restatement Second of Contracts, authorizing rescission for unilateral mistake of fact where enforcement would be unconscionable, is consistent with our previous decisions, we adopt the rule as California law.

entries.disposition_note: READ AND ENCODED. Supplies both Restatement sections verbatim, the four California elements, and fixture 7 -- the corpus's sharpest divergence. Opens fork F-US1 on whether the American column states the Restatement rule or a State's law. Re-retrieving it from a pinnable source also exposed a misquotation that had reached the encoding; see the source bundle's note on donovan-2001.
